# Overview

This exercise follows chapter 18 of the book and Lesson 8. A market area, or trade area, is the area a store draws its customers from. The Huff model estimates the chance that people living in one place shop at each store. The chance goes up with how attractive the store is and down with how far away it is, compared with all the competing stores.

The setting is a fast-food franchise with 28 stores in Taichung City, Taiwan. I compute the Huff probabilities from every village to every store, map the trade area of one store, and use the village populations to estimate how many customers each store should get. Then I compare that estimate with the stores' actual sales.

# Loading the Packages

**MCI** is the new package. Its `huff.shares()` computes the Huff probabilities and `shares.total()` adds them up for each store. **sf**, **tmap**, **tidyverse** and **ggstatsplot** do the same jobs as before, and I add **knitr** for tables.

```{r}
#| output: false
pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, MCI, tmap, ggstatsplot, knitr)
```

# Importing the Data

## Importing the Geospatial Data

`st_read()` of **sf** reads the three shapefiles, the store locations, the district boundaries and the village boundaries.

```{r}
stores <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "STORES_TC")
town <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "TOWN_TC")
village <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "VILLAGE_TC")
```

All three layers are in TWD97 / TM2 zone 121, EPSG 3826, a projected system in metres. I check the codes directly instead of reading them off the printout.

```{r}
c(stores = st_crs(stores)$epsg,
  town = st_crs(town)$epsg,
  village = st_crs(village)$epsg)
```

There are `r nrow(stores)` stores, `r nrow(town)` districts and `r nrow(village)` villages.

`tm_shape()` and `tm_polygons()` of **tmap** draw the districts and villages, and `tm_dots()` adds the stores.

The stores sit close together in the central districts. A few stand alone at the edges, such as TG in Dajia in the north and EH in Dongshi in the east. `r sum(lengths(st_intersects(town, stores)) == 0)` of the `r nrow(town)` districts have no store at all.

## Where I differ from the book
The book draws this overview with `tmap_mode("view")` as an interactive web map. I use static plot mode with the store codes as labels, so the map shows without loading web tiles and I can see which code is which store. The thick lines are the district boundaries and the thin ones are the villages.
:::

## Importing the Aspatial Data

`read_csv()` of **readr** reads the 2019 population by village and the store sales records.

```{r}
pop2019 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/pop2019.csv")
store_sales <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Store_sales_data.csv")
```

```{r}
summary(store_sales)
```

`H_CNT`, `P_CNT`, `M_CNT` and `F_CNT` in pop2019 are the number of households, the total population, and the male and female population.

::: {.callout-important}
## Check that caught something
The sales file has `r format(nrow(store_sales), big.mark = ",")` rows, but they are not all from the 28 Taichung stores. I count the store codes in it.

```{r}
c(codes_in_sales_file = n_distinct(store_sales$`Store Code`, na.rm = TRUE),
  rows_without_code = sum(is.na(store_sales$`Store Code`)),
  codes_in_Taichung = sum(unique(store_sales$`Store Code`) %in% stores$Store_CD),
  Taichung_stores_missing = sum(!stores$Store_CD %in% store_sales$`Store Code`))
```

The file covers `r n_distinct(store_sales[["Store Code"]], na.rm = TRUE)` store codes, so it seems to come from the whole chain, and `r sum(is.na(store_sales[["Store Code"]]))` rows have no store code at all. Only `r sum(unique(store_sales[["Store Code"]]) %in% stores$Store_CD)` are in Taichung, and every Taichung store has sales. The book's `left_join()` onto the stores keeps only those 28, so the other stores and the rows without a code drop out without any warning. That is what we want here, but the `summary()` above describes the whole file, not the 28 stores.
:::

# Data Preparation

## Aggregating the Store Sales

`group_by()` and `summarise()` of **dplyr** add up the bills and the sales amount for each store code.

```{r}
store_sales_aggre <- store_sales %>%
  group_by(`Store Code`) %>%
  summarise(
    "Total_Bill" = sum(Bills, na.rm = TRUE),
    "Total_Sales" = sum(Amount, na.rm = TRUE))
```

## Joining the Sales to the Stores

`left_join()` appends the totals to the stores, and `mutate()` gives every store a size of 100.

```{r}
stores <- stores %>%
  left_join(store_sales_aggre,
            by = join_by(Store_CD == `Store Code`)) %>%
  mutate(Store_size = 100)
```

```{r}
summary(stores)
```

There are no missing values. Total sales run from `r format(min(stores$Total_Sales), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(stores$Total_Sales), big.mark = ",")`, so the best store sells about `r round(max(stores$Total_Sales) / min(stores$Total_Sales), 1)` times as much as the weakest.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
`Store_size` is the store's attractiveness in the Huff model. The book sets it to 100 for every store because the data has no real measure of size. In the lesson's formula the attractiveness appears on the top and the bottom of the probability, so when every store has the same value it cancels out. The probabilities then depend on distance only. Everything that follows is a model of geography, where a store wins customers just by being nearer than its rivals.
:::

## Tidying the Population Data

Before joining pop2019 to the villages, I check that the join fields look the same.

```{r}
glimpse(pop2019)
```

```{r}
glimpse(village)
```

`V_ID` in pop2019 has a dash, like 66000110-002, while `VILLCODE` in the village layer does not. `str_remove_all()` of **stringr** removes the dash.

```{r}
pop2019 <- pop2019 %>%
  mutate(V_ID = str_remove_all(V_ID, "-"))
```

Now `left_join()` appends the population to the villages.

```{r}
village <- village %>%
  left_join(pop2019,
            by = join_by(VILLCODE == V_ID))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Check that caught something
pop2019 has `r nrow(pop2019)` villages but the village layer has `r nrow(village)`. A left join keeps the rows of the village layer, so any village that is only in pop2019 is dropped without a message. I check which ones.

```{r}
pop_only <- pop2019 %>%
  filter(!V_ID %in% village$VILLCODE)

pop_only %>%
  group_by(TOWN_ID, TOWN) %>%
  summarise(villages = n(), people = sum(P_CNT), .groups = "drop") %>%
  kable()

as.character(unique(pop_only$TOWN_ID)) %in% as.character(town$TOWNCODE)
```

All `r nrow(pop_only)` dropped villages are in one district, `r unique(pop_only$TOWN)`, which is Heping District, with `r format(sum(pop_only$P_CNT), big.mark = ",")` people. Its code is not in the town layer either, which has `r nrow(town)` districts. So Heping, the mountain area in the east of Taichung, has been left out of the study area. It holds only `r round(sum(pop_only$P_CNT) / sum(pop2019$P_CNT) * 100, 1)` percent of the people and has no store, so leaving it out changes little. But it means the analysis covers `r nrow(town)` districts, not the whole city.
:::

## Checking for Missing Values

```{r}
summary(village)
```

Five villages have no population. I look at them before removing them.

```{r}
village %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(is.na(P_CNT)) %>%
  select(VILLCODE, TOWNID, VILLNAME, VILLENG) %>%
  kable()
```

Their codes end in S01 to S03 instead of a number, and they have no village name. They seem to be special areas without residents rather than villages with missing data, so removing them is safe. `filter()` removes them.

```{r}
village <- village %>%
  filter(!is.na(P_CNT))
```

```{r}
any(is.na(village$H_CNT))
any(is.na(village$P_CNT))
any(is.na(village$M_CNT))
any(is.na(village$F_CNT))
```

All four are `FALSE`. `r nrow(village)` villages with `r format(sum(village$P_CNT), big.mark = ",")` people are left.

# Computing the Distance Matrix

Each village needs one point to measure distance from. `st_point_on_surface()` of **sf** gives a point that is always inside the village, and `st_distance()` computes the straight-line distance from each of those points to each store.

```{r}
village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)
dim(distmat)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
The book says it uses the centroid of each village, but the code uses `st_point_on_surface()`. The two are not the same. A centroid is the centre of mass, and for a curved or oddly shaped village it can fall outside the village. I count how often that happens here.

```{r}
village_centroid <- st_centroid(village)
centroid_outside <- sum(!diag(st_within(village_centroid, village, sparse = FALSE)))
centroid_outside
```

`r centroid_outside` village centroids fall outside their own village. The point on surface avoids this, so the code is right and only the text is loose.
:::

The matrix has one row per village and one column per store. The book names the rows and columns with the codes and turns the matrix into a long table with `pivot_longer()` of **tidyr**, one row per village and store pair.

```{r}
rownames(distmat) <- village$`VILLCODE`
colnames(distmat) <- stores$`Store_CD`

distmat_long <- distmat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "VILLCODE") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -VILLCODE,
    names_to = "Store_CD",
    values_to = "distance") %>%
  mutate(distance = as.numeric(distance))
```

There are `r format(nrow(distmat_long), big.mark = ",")` pairs, `r nrow(village)` villages × `r nrow(stores)` stores. The distances are in metres and run from `r round(min(distmat_long$distance))` m to `r round(max(distmat_long$distance) / 1000, 1)` km. Half of the villages have a store within `r round(median(apply(distmat, 1, min)) / 1000, 1)` km.

# Preparing the Interaction Matrix

**MCI** needs a long table with the origin, the store, the attractiveness and the distance. `left_join()` adds `Store_size` to each pair, and `relocate()` moves the distance to the last column.

```{r}
interaction_matrix <- distmat_long %>%
  left_join(
    stores %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      select(Store_CD, Store_size),
    by = "Store_CD") %>%
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())
```

```{r}
summary(interaction_matrix)
```

# Computing the Huff Model

`huff.shares()` takes the interaction matrix and the names of the origin, store, attractiveness and distance columns.

```{r}
huff_share <- huff.shares(
  interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
  "Store_size", "distance")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
The lesson writes the utility as U~ij~ = A~j~^α^ d~ij~^−λ^, and the probability as p~ij~ = U~ij~ ÷ ΣU~ij~ over all stores. The book does not set the weights, so I read the source of `huff.shares()` to see the defaults. `gamma = 1` is the lesson's α, and `lambda = -2` with `dtype = "pow"` gives d^−2^. **MCI** writes the exponent with its minus sign, while the lesson puts the minus in the formula, so λ = 2 in the lesson is `lambda = -2` here.

The source also showed two smaller things. The output is sorted by village and then store, not in the input order. And the column `sum_U_ij` is built with `rbind()` of lists, so it comes back as a list column instead of numbers. It does not affect `p_ij`, but a numeric summary of that column would fail.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Check that caught something
Each village's probabilities should add up to one across the 28 stores.

```{r}
huff_share %>%
  group_by(VILLCODE) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(p_ij)) %>%
  summarise(lowest = min(total), highest = max(total))
```

They do. This also shows a built-in assumption of the model. Every resident of every village is a customer of one of these 28 stores. Nobody eats at a rival chain or stays home, however far the nearest store is.
:::

## Trade Area of a Single Store

The book filters the probabilities of one store, store BT, joins them to the villages and pulls out the store's location.

```{r}
market_share <- huff_share %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")

Trade_area <- village %>%
  left_join(market_share, by = "VILLCODE")

selected_store <- stores %>%
  filter(Store_CD == "BT")
```

I compute ten quantile classes myself and label them with two significant figures, so the small probabilities are readable.

::: panel-tabset

```{r}
bt <- Trade_area %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(expected = p_ij * P_CNT)

c(villages_above_half = sum(bt$p_ij > 0.5),
  farthest_of_those_m = round(max(bt$distance[bt$p_ij > 0.5])),
  median_probability = round(median(bt$p_ij), 3),
  pct_customers_within_3km = round(sum(bt$expected[bt$distance <= 3000]) / sum(bt$expected) * 100),
  pct_customers_beyond_5km = round(sum(bt$expected[bt$distance > 5000]) / sum(bt$expected) * 100))
```

BT has a probability above one half in only `r sum(bt$p_ij > 0.5)` villages, all within `r round(max(bt$distance[bt$p_ij > 0.5]))` m of the store. In the median village it is `r round(median(bt$p_ij), 3)`. Still, only `r round(sum(bt$expected[bt$distance <= 3000]) / sum(bt$expected) * 100)` percent of its expected customers live within 3 km, and `r round(sum(bt$expected[bt$distance > 5000]) / sum(bt$expected) * 100)` percent live more than 5 km away. Each far village gives BT only a small share, but there are many of them. A Huff trade area has no edge, it fades out across the whole city. The map also shows that the far eastern hills give BT a higher share than the western plain does, although they are further away. Every store is far from the hills, so the distances differ little and the customers there are split almost evenly. The grey patches are the five areas without residents that were removed earlier.

::: {.callout-caution}
## Where I differ from the book
The book's text says it selects store TG but the code filters BT, so I follow the code. I compute and label the quantile classes myself, put the legend outside the map, and add the other 27 stores as small white dots, so the reader can see why BT's probability drops where it does. BT is drawn in orange instead of red to stand out against the blue scale. I left out the book's `tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)`, since borders have no fill and the villages already have outlines, and `tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)`, which uses the old v3 argument.
:::

## Store Sales Analysis

The lesson multiplies each probability by the market potential of the village to get the expected flow of customers, E~ij~ = p~ij~ × C~i~, and adds the flows up for each store. Here the market potential is the village population. `left_join()` adds `P_CNT` to the Huff output.

```{r}
huff_share_pp <- huff_share %>%
  left_join(village %>%
              st_drop_geometry() %>%
              select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE") %>%
  relocate(distance, .after = last_col())
```

`shares.total()` of **MCI** computes the expected customers of each store, `sum_E_j`, and its share of the market, `share_j`.

```{r}
huff_total <- shares.total(
  huff_share_pp, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
  "p_ij", "P_CNT")
```

`left_join()` appends the estimate to the stores.

```{r}
store_sales_est <- stores %>%
  left_join(huff_total,
            by = join_by("Store_CD" == "suppliers_single"))
```

`ggscatterstats()` of **ggstatsplot** plots the estimate against the actual sales and adds a correlation test.

```{r}
store_sales_nongeom <- store_sales_est %>%
  st_drop_geometry()
```

::: panel-tabset
## The Plot

```{r}
huff_cor <- cor.test(store_sales_nongeom$sum_E_j,
                     store_sales_nongeom$Total_Sales)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning diary
The Pearson correlation is `r round(huff_cor$estimate, 2)`, with a p-value of `r signif(huff_cor$p.value, 2)`. So a model that knows only where the stores and the people are already explains about `r round(huff_cor$estimate^2 * 100)` percent of the variation in sales.

The two axes are in different units. `sum_E_j` counts people, and it always adds up to the total population of `r format(sum(huff_total$sum_E_j), big.mark = ",")`, because every resident is shared out among the stores. `Total_Sales` is money. A correlation does not care about units, so the comparison is fair, but the estimate cannot be read as a sales forecast. To get money, the population would have to be multiplied by spending per person, which the lesson calls purchasing power.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Where I differ from the book
I set the colours myself, since `ggscatterstats()` draws its side histograms in green and orange by default. I also added axis titles, comma labels for the large numbers and a title that states the finding.
:::

The book ends by turning the probabilities into a wide table, one row per village and one column per store, which is easier to read for a single village.

```{r}
huff_share_wider <- huff_share %>%
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD,
              values_from = p_ij)

dim(huff_share_wider)
kable(head(huff_share_wider[, 1:8]), digits = 3)
```

# Beyond the Exercise

## Fitting the Distance Decay to the Actual Sales

The book uses the default λ = 2 without testing it. Lesson 8 says the exponent sets how fast the pull of a store decays with distance, and that it is a weighting parameter to be estimated. The stores' actual sales give a way to estimate it. For each λ, I compute each store's expected share of the market, the lesson's M~j~, and compare it with the store's actual share of total sales. Using shares instead of totals puts both sides on the same scale, so the people versus money problem in the diary above goes away.

A loop over `huff.shares()` would be slow, so I compute the same formula with matrices. With every store at size 100 the attractiveness cancels, so it is left out.

```{r}
dist_wide <- distmat_long %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD, values_from = distance)
D <- as.matrix(select(dist_wide, -VILLCODE))
pop <- village$P_CNT[match(dist_wide$VILLCODE, village$VILLCODE)]

actual_share <- stores$Total_Sales[match(colnames(D), stores$Store_CD)]
actual_share <- setNames(actual_share / sum(actual_share), colnames(D))

huff_est_share <- function(lambda) {
  U <- D^lambda
  P <- U / rowSums(U)
  E <- colSums(P * pop)
  E / sum(E)
}
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Check that caught something
Before using my own function, I check it against the package. With λ = 2 it should give exactly the `share_j` that `shares.total()` gave.

```{r}
check_share <- huff_est_share(-2)[huff_total$suppliers_single]
max(abs(check_share - huff_total$share_j))
```

The largest difference is `r format(signif(max(abs(check_share - huff_total$share_j)), 2), scientific = TRUE)`, which is only rounding error, so the two agree.
:::

I try λ from 0.2 to 4 in steps of 0.1 and compute the sum of squared differences between the expected and actual shares.

```{r}
calibration <- tibble(lambda = seq(-0.2, -4, by = -0.1)) %>%
  mutate(sum_sq_diff = map_dbl(lambda,
                               ~ sum((huff_est_share(.x) - actual_share)^2)),
         correlation = map_dbl(lambda,
                               ~ cor(huff_est_share(.x), actual_share)))

best <- slice_min(calibration, sum_sq_diff)
book <- filter(calibration, lambda == -2)
equal_split <- sum((1 / length(actual_share) - actual_share)^2)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative explored
The best fit is λ = `r -best$lambda`. It lowers the squared differences by `r round((1 - best$sum_sq_diff / book$sum_sq_diff) * 100)` percent compared with λ = 2, and the correlation with actual shares rises from `r round(book$correlation, 2)` to `r round(best$correlation, 2)`. A smaller λ means distance puts people off less, so a store draws more custom from further away than the default assumes. That is believable for fast food in a city where many people drive or ride a scooter.

The gain is real but limited. Giving every store the same share, 1 in 28, has squared differences of `r signif(equal_split, 2)`. The best Huff model brings that down to `r signif(best$sum_sq_diff, 2)`, so it removes only `r round((1 - best$sum_sq_diff / equal_split) * 100)` percent of the differences between stores. Distance alone cannot explain why some stores sell twice as much as others. **MCI** has `huff.lambda()` for this kind of fit, but it compares the expected totals with the actual totals directly, which only makes sense if the market potential is in the same unit as the sales. With people on one side and money on the other, its answer would be meaningless, so I compared shares instead.
:::

## Which Stores Sell More Than Their Location Predicts

If the Huff model with the fitted λ captures what location alone is worth, then the gap between a store's actual share and its expected share is what the location does not explain. That is useful to a franchise, because it points to stores that do better or worse than their position suggests. I divide the actual share by the expected share and group the stores into three classes.

```{r}
store_perf <- stores %>%
  mutate(expected_share = huff_est_share(best$lambda)[Store_CD],
         actual_share = actual_share[Store_CD],
         ratio = actual_share / expected_share,
         performance = cut(ratio, breaks = c(0, 0.75, 1.25, Inf),
                           labels = c("Sells well below its location",
                                      "Within 25 percent of its location",
                                      "Sells well above its location")))

store_perf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(ratio) %>%
  select(Store_CD, Store_Name, expected_share, actual_share, ratio) %>%
  slice(c(1:6, (n() - 4):n())) %>%
  kable(digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 2))
```

## Alternative explored
The ratios split into clear groups. `r sum(store_perf$ratio < 0.75)` stores, `r paste(store_perf$Store_CD[order(store_perf$ratio)][1:sum(store_perf$ratio < 0.75)], collapse = ", ")`, sell less than half of the share their location predicts, with ratios from `r round(min(store_perf$ratio), 2)` to `r round(max(store_perf$ratio[store_perf$ratio < 0.75]), 2)`. The next lowest store is at `r round(min(store_perf$ratio[store_perf$ratio >= 0.75]), 2)`, so there is a real gap. At the other end, `r sum(store_perf$ratio > 1.25)` stores sell at least a quarter more than predicted.

TG and EH are the stores that stand alone at the edge of the city. The Huff model gives them almost all of the large rural areas around them, because there is no other store nearby, but their sales are among the lowest. This fits the assumption found earlier. The model makes every resident a customer of some store, while many people far from any store probably eat elsewhere. The data cannot say why the other three underperform. Possible reasons include a smaller store, a poor site within the village, a newer opening during the sales period, or strong competition from other brands, which this model does not include. A franchise analyst would start by visiting these five.
:::

## Market Areas of All 28 Stores

The book maps the trade area of one store. A franchise would also want to see all the market areas together. I give each village to the store with the highest probability, using the book's λ = 2, and merge the villages of each store into one area with `summarise()`, which unions the geometries.

```{r}
dominant <- huff_share %>%
  group_by(VILLCODE) %>%
  slice_max(p_ij, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(VILLCODE, dominant_store = Store_CD, max_p = p_ij)

village_dom <- village %>%
  left_join(dominant, by = "VILLCODE")

market_areas <- village_dom %>%
  group_by(dominant_store) %>%
  summarise()

nearest <- huff_share %>%
  group_by(VILLCODE) %>%
  slice_min(distance, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

c(market_areas = nrow(market_areas),
  pct_dominant_is_nearest = mean(dominant$dominant_store ==
                                   nearest$Store_CD[match(dominant$VILLCODE, nearest$VILLCODE)]) * 100,
  pct_villages_no_majority = round(mean(dominant$max_p < 0.5) * 100),
  pct_people_no_majority = round(sum(village_dom$P_CNT[village_dom$max_p < 0.5]) /
                                   sum(village_dom$P_CNT) * 100))
```

The colour shows the highest probability in each village, so dark villages belong clearly to one store and pale villages are shared between several. The black lines are the market area boundaries.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative explored
In `r round(mean(dominant$max_p < 0.5) * 100)` percent of the villages, home to `r round(sum(village_dom$P_CNT[village_dom$max_p < 0.5]) / sum(village_dom$P_CNT) * 100)` percent of the people, no store has a probability above one half. Each store has a small dark core where it clearly wins. The pale villages fall into two groups. Between stores in the centre, the customers are split because several stores are close by. In the eastern and southern hills, every store is far away, so the distances differ little and the customers are split almost evenly too. The darkest large areas are around TG and EH, which have no near rival.

The market areas are exactly the nearest-store areas. In every village the store with the highest probability is also the nearest one. This follows from giving every store the same size. With equal attractiveness, the only thing that can make one store beat another is distance, so the Huff market areas become the same as Thiessen polygons built on the villages. The Huff model only adds something new to the boundaries when the stores differ in attractiveness. What it does add even here is the shading, which shows how strongly each village belongs to its store, something a nearest-store map cannot show.
:::

# Limitations

- Every store has the same attractiveness, so the model is about distance only. Store size, opening hours, parking or a drive-through would all change the results.
- The distances are straight lines from one point in each village. Road distance or travel time would be more realistic, especially across rivers and hills.
- Every resident is assumed to be a customer of one of the 28 stores. Other brands, home cooking and people who never buy fast food are ignored, which inflates the expected customers of stores at the edge of the city.
- Market potential is the total population. Spending on fast food differs with age and income, so a young, busy district is worth more per person than an old rural one.
- The sales data has no dates, so it is not clear what period it covers, or whether every store was open for all of it.
- Heping District is not in the study area, and people near the city boundary who shop in neighbouring cities, or come in from them, are not counted.

# Reflections

Here are four things I learned from this exercise.

**A constant can quietly remove a whole part of a model.** Setting every store's size to 100 looks harmless, but it cancels the attractiveness out of the formula. The trade areas then became the same as nearest-store areas. Before accepting a placeholder value, I will check what it does to the formula.

**Joins can drop data in both directions.** The sales file held `r n_distinct(store_sales[["Store Code"]], na.rm = TRUE)` stores and the population file had 8 villages that are not on the map. Both joins dropped rows without any message. Counting rows and keys on both sides of a join is a habit worth keeping.

**Default parameters deserve a test when data is available.** The actual sales let me fit the distance decay, and λ = `r -best$lambda` fitted better than the default of 2. The model still left most of the differences between stores unexplained, which is useful to know too.

**The leftover is often the interesting part.** The most useful output for a franchise was not the trade area map but the stores that sell far below what their location predicts. The model is most helpful as a baseline to compare the real stores against.
